name: Oaxaca
tagline: Mexico's food and craft capital: seven moles, mezcal, indigenous markets, a baroque city and the Zapotec ruins of Monte Albán above it.
highlight: Monte Albán at opening, then mole and mezcal in the old city that evening.
shortDescription: A colourful colonial city in the Sierra Madre del Sur, the heart of Zapotec and Mixtec culture, with the country's best food, mezcal and handicrafts, and ruins and craft villages in the valleys around it.
metaDescription: An Oaxaca travel guide: Monte Albán, Santo Domingo, markets, mole and mezcal, Hierve el Agua, Mitla and craft villages, Día de Muertos, where to stay and a three-day plan.
knownFor: Mole, mezcal, markets, Monte Albán, Día de Muertos, crafts
goodFor: Food, crafts, culture, ruins, day trips

image.file: File:Church of Santo Domingo in Oaxaca.jpg
image.alt: The baroque facade of the Church of Santo Domingo de Guzmán in Oaxaca

intro: Oaxaca sits in a high valley in southern Mexico, where the Zapotec and Mixtec civilisations flourished for two thousand years before the Spaniards arrived. About a third of the state's people still speak an indigenous language, and the city's markets, craft villages and cooking reflect a living culture that is more visible than almost anywhere else in Mexico.

The historic centre and the ruins of Monte Albán are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The centre is a grid of low, colourful colonial buildings in green volcanic stone, with a baroque church, Santo Domingo, and its former convent, now a museum, at its heart. Around the Zócalo, cafés and mezcal bars fill the arcades in the evening.

Oaxaca is above all a food city. It claims seven classic moles, quesillo string cheese, tlayudas, chapulines (grasshoppers), chocolate and the mezcal of the surrounding villages. A day here can revolve around a market breakfast, a cooking class and a long dinner, and the valleys around the city offer ruins, waterfalls and weaving villages.

whyVisit.intro: Oaxaca is the most rewarding city in Mexico for food, craft and living indigenous culture.

points.title: Mexico's best food
points.text: Moles, tlayudas, memelas, tamales and chocolate made and eaten as they have been for centuries.

points.title: Mezcal
points.text: Small producers in the valleys distil mezcal from wild and cultivated agave using traditional methods, and tastings are easy to arrange.

points.title: Markets and crafts
points.text: Black pottery, alebrijes, woven rugs and embroidered clothing are made in villages a short drive from the city.

points.title: Ancient Zapotec sites
points.text: Monte Albán, Mitla and Yagul show a civilisation that flourished from about 500 BCE.

points.title: Día de Muertos
points.text: Oaxaca's celebration of 1–2 November, with altars, cemetery vigils and parades, is one of the most vivid in the country.

attractionsIntro: The centre is compact, and the valleys around it fill several more days.

attractions.name: The Zócalo and the Cathedral

image.file: File:Kiosk of the Zocalo of Oaxaca City.jpg
image.alt: The kiosk in the Zócalo of Oaxaca City

attractions.text: The main square is shaded by laurel trees and lined with arcaded cafés. It comes alive in the evening with musicians, vendors and families.
attractions.tip: Have a drink at an arcade table and watch the evening unfold.

attractions.name: Santo Domingo and the Cultural Centre
attractions.text: A gilded baroque church, with an intricate interior, and its adjoining monastery, which houses the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca and a botanical garden.
attractions.tip: Visit the museum for the Monte Albán tomb 7 treasure.

attractions.name: Monte Albán

image.file: File:Group of visitors at Monte Alban 1976.jpg
image.alt: Visitors on the great plaza of the ancient Zapotec city of Monte Albán

attractions.text: A Zapotec capital on a levelled mountaintop above the city, with a great plaza, pyramids, an observatory and carved stones. It was occupied from about 500 BCE to 800 CE.
attractions.tip: Go at opening, and take a guide or read up first.

attractions.name: The markets
attractions.text: The Benito Juárez and 20 de Noviembre markets are the place for smoked meat, mole pastes, chocolate, cheese and mezcal. The Tlacolula market, on Sundays, is one of the largest in the region.
attractions.tip: Try tlayudas and the smoke-grill corridor in 20 de Noviembre.

attractions.name: Hierve el Agua
attractions.text: Petrified waterfalls of mineral formation on a mountain edge, with natural infinity pools and views over the valley. About 90 minutes from the city.

attractions.name: Mitla and Zapotec sites
attractions.text: A religious centre with intricate geometric stone mosaics on its palaces, and the nearby ruins of Yagul.
attractions.tip: Visit on the way to Hierve el Agua.

attractions.name: Craft villages
attractions.text: San Bartolo Coyotepec (black pottery), Teotitlán del Valle (wool rugs), and San Martín Tilcajete and Arrazola (alebrijes, painted wooden animals).

thingsToDoIntro: Oaxaca is a city for eating slowly and learning how things are made.

thingsToDo.title: Take a cooking class
thingsToDo.text: Start at a market, buy ingredients and learn to make mole, salsas and tortillas.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a mezcal distillery
thingsToDo.text: See agave roasted in earthen pits, crushed by stone wheel and distilled in clay or copper stills, and taste the results.
thingsToDo.tip: Go with a guide, and do not drink and drive.

thingsToDo.title: Spend a day in the craft villages
thingsToDo.text: Watch weavers, potters and carvers at work in family workshops around the valley.
thingsToDo.tip: Hire a driver for the day.

thingsToDo.title: Eat at the market
thingsToDo.text: Breakfast on tamales and atole, lunch on tlayudas, and dinner at a market grill.
thingsToDo.tip: Go before noon for the best selection.

thingsToDo.title: Be there for Día de Muertos
thingsToDo.text: Cemetery vigils, altars, parades and comparsas fill the city in the days around 1 and 2 November.
thingsToDo.tip: Book accommodation months ahead, and be respectful.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the Andador Turístico
thingsToDo.text: A pedestrian street of galleries, shops and cafés from the Zócalo to Santo Domingo.

foodIntro: Oaxaca is the culinary capital of Mexico. Its food is built on corn, beans, chiles, chocolate and cheese, with dishes that differ from village to village.

foods.name: Mole negro and the seven moles
foods.text: Rich sauces of chiles, spices, seeds, chocolate and fruit. Mole negro is the most famous, but the others include coloradito, amarillo, verde, chichilo, rojo and manchamanteles.

foods.name: Tlayudas
foods.text: Large, crisp tortillas topped with beans, quesillo, tasajo and salsa, grilled over charcoal.

foods.name: Quesillo and memelas
foods.text: Oaxaca's string cheese, wound into balls, and thick corn tortillas with beans and cheese.

foods.name: Chapulines
foods.text: Toasted grasshoppers seasoned with chile, lime and garlic, sold by the scoop in the markets.

foods.name: Chocolate and hot chocolate
foods.text: Ground with sugar, cinnamon and almonds and served as a hot drink, often with bread.

foods.name: Mezcal
foods.text: Distilled from agave, with smoky and complex flavours, served neat with orange and worm salt.
foods.whereToTry: Bars and tasting rooms in the centre.

accommodation.intro: Stay in the historic centre, in a restored colonial house with a courtyard, so that you can walk everywhere.

areas.name: The historic centre
areas.text: Boutique hotels and guesthouses in old houses around the Zócalo and Santo Domingo.

areas.name: Jalatlaco and Xochimilco neighbourhoods
areas.text: Small colourful neighbourhoods a few blocks from the centre, with cafés and guesthouses.

gettingThere.intro: Oaxaca is 460 km from Mexico City by road, and flights are the easiest way.

options.text: About an hour, with several daily flights, at low fares.

options.mode: Bus from Mexico City or Puebla
options.text: First-class buses take 6–7 hours from Mexico City, and about 5 from Puebla. Night buses are cheaper but slower.
Small planes and mountain buses link Oaxaca with Puerto Escondido and Huatulco, with a winding road of 6–9 hours.
options.detail: Flights are quicker and more comfortable.

gettingAround.intro: The centre is walkable, and taxis, colectivos and tours cover the valleys.

options.text: Everything in the centre is within 20 minutes on foot.
Cheap taxis and shared vans go to Monte Albán, Mitla and the craft villages.
A driver for a day is inexpensive and efficient for visiting several villages.

bestTime.headline: October–April
bestTime.summary: Oaxaca sits at 1,550 m and has a mild climate, with a wet season from June to September. The dry months are the most comfortable.

seasons.text: Dry and sunny, with cool nights. The best time, and the high season.
Warm to hot, with the first rains.
Green, with afternoon showers. Quiet and cheaper. The Guelaguetza festival in July draws crowds.
Clear and pleasant. Día de Muertos makes early November the busiest time.

bestTime.avoid: Día de Muertos and the Guelaguetza in July if you want quiet, and Semana Santa.

itinerary.title: Three days in Oaxaca
itinerary.intro: The centre and markets on the first day, Monte Albán and a cooking class on the second, the valleys on the third.

days.title: The centre and markets
days.afternoon: The markets and lunch of tlayudas.
days.evening: Mezcal and dinner near the Zócalo.

days.title: Monte Albán and cooking
days.afternoon: A cooking class and market visit.

days.title: The valleys
days.morning: Teotitlán del Valle's weavers and a mezcal distillery.
days.evening: A last dinner in the city.

tipsIntro: Oaxaca is easy and friendly, and a few tips help.
tips: Book Día de Muertos and the Guelaguetza months ahead.
Go to Monte Albán early, before the sun and the buses.
Eat at busy market stalls and street grills, and drink bottled water.
Buy crafts directly from the makers, and ask before photographing people.
Try mezcal slowly and know the difference between artisanal and industrial bottles.
Bring a light jacket, as evenings are cool.
Avoid driving at night on mountain roads.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Oaxaca?
faq.a: Three to four for the city and Monte Albán, and a few more to include the valleys and a cooking class.
The city and the main tourist sites are generally safe for visitors, though protests and road blockades can occur in the state. Check your government's advice and local news.
A spirit distilled from agave, often from a smoky, earth-roasted heart. Oaxaca produces most of Mexico's mezcal, and tequila is a type of mezcal made only from blue agave.
A festival of indigenous dance and music held on two Mondays in July, at the Cerro del Fortín amphitheatre. Book well ahead.

faq.q: How do I get to Monte Albán?
faq.a: By taxi, tour or the local bus from the city centre, about 20–30 minutes.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit Oaxaca?
faq.a: November to April for dry weather, though the summer green season is quiet and pleasant.
